query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A predictive approach that decouples lattice and electronic heat transport—by combining advanced density-functional theory (DFT) with on‐the‐fly machine learning corrections for anharmonic phonon scattering and separate Boltzmann transport calculations for electrons—will yield thermal conductivity predictions for HfNbTaTiZr within ±20% of experimental values, outperforming older Debye‐temperature based models that typically err by more than ±50%.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk, high-purity HfNbTaTiZr alloy; samples include nearly defect-free crystals and ones with controlled 1 wt.% oxygen impurities as in reported experiments.
generation.intervention: Implement a computational framework that separately computes the lattice thermal conductivity (using DFT enhanced by machine learning to capture atomic-scale anharmonic effects) and the electronic thermal conductivity (via semiclassical Boltzmann transport theory), ensuring that the two contributions are not conflated.
generation.conditions: Predictions are made under conditions spanning: • Low temperature (<200 K) where lattice and electronic contributions are comparable, and • Elevated temperatures (300–1200 K) matching the experimental conditions with oxygen-doped specimens.
generation.structural_mediator: The approach mediates at the atomic scale by explicitly incorporating the effects of local heterogeneities and anharmonic scattering that arise in complex, concentrated alloys.
generation.mechanism: By distinguishing the scattering mechanisms and transport paths for phonons and electrons, the method more accurately estimates each contribution. The enhanced DFT and machine learning component corrects for limitations of simpler Debye approximations, while independent Boltzmann transport calculations avoid conflating the two channels.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will predict a total thermal conductivity that falls in the 10–17 W/(K·m) range (with lattice and electronic components closely matching independent low-temperature and high-temperature measurements) and will reduce prediction error from >50% (in older models) to within ±20% of experimental values.
generation.baseline: Earlier approaches that rely on overall approximations—using Debye temperatures and unified treatment of phonon/electron transport—yield predictions with errors >50% and do not capture the decoupled contributions observed in experiments.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to samples of HfNbTaTiZr with controlled stoichiometry and minor oxygen impurities (up to ~1 wt.%). Its applicability may be limited in highly disordered or defect-rich samples where additional scattering mechanisms play a dominant role.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement (i.e., the reduction to ±20% error) is based on extrapolations from analogous systems and may vary with sample microstructure and impurity distributions. Further, the separation of phonon and electron contributions could be sensitive to details not fully captured in the model.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one nearly defect-free and one with controlled 1 wt.% oxygen impurity. Perform independent measurements of lattice and electronic thermal conductivity—using low-temperature (below 200 K) scanning thermal measurements for phonon contributions and high-temperature (300–1200 K) total conductivity measurements combined with electrical transport (e.g., Hall effect) for electronic contributions. Compare these experimental values against predictions from the new decoupled model.
measurements: Electrical conductivity and Seebeck coefficient for electronic transport
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the separate lattice and electronic conductivity predictions, as well as the total thermal conductivity, deviate by more than ±20% from the corresponding experimental measurements across the specified temperature ranges, and if no systematic improvement over Debye-based models is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Investigation of PbSnTeSe High-Entropy Thermoelectric Alloy: A DFT Approach

Abstract: Thermoelectric materials have attracted extensive attention because they can directly convert waste heat into electric energy. As a brand-new method of alloying, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in the fields of materials science and engineering. Recent researches have found that HEAs could be potentially good thermoelectric (TE) materials. In this study, special quasi-random structures (SQS) of PbSnTeSe high-entropy alloys consisting of 64 atoms have been generated. The thermoelectric transport properties of the highest-entropy PbSnTeSe-optimized structure were investigated by combining calculations from first-principles density-functional theory and on-the-fly machine learning with the semiclassical Boltzmann transport theory and Green–Kubo theory. The results demonstrate that PbSnTeSe HEA has a very low lattice thermal conductivity. The electrical conductivity, thermal electronic conductivity and Seebeck coefficient have been evaluated for both n-type and p-type doping.
